item.title: STAT+: FDA rejects Capricor Therapeutics’ Duchenne therapy, a decision that was a long time coming
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The Food and Drug Administration said Friday that it had rejected a cell therapy intended for patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy developed by Capricor Therapeutics.

The decision to block the treatment, called deramiocel, from reaching the market should have been an easy one for regulators to make. The targeted patient population — teenagers and young men with Duchenne who had already lost the ability to walk — have few treatment options today. Deramiocel didn’t help them either. Capricor conducted two randomized clinical trials. Both failed to show deramiocel could stave off heart failure or preserve muscle function in their arms.

But nothing is straightforward when it comes to regulating drugs for Duchenne, a progressive, muscle-wasting disease.

item.title: Flu vaccine effectiveness often weaker than advertised, study finds
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Flu vaccine effectiveness often weaker than advertised, study finds

Sadie Harley

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

New research suggests health officials may be overselling the protective power of the annual flu shot—but that doesn't mean folks should skip it, researchers added. The new analysis finds the influenza vaccine is often less protective than the 40% to 60% effectiveness against infection that's routinely stated, according to researchers from the University of Maryland.

In many seasons, it may not even match current circulating strains, they noted.

"The 40% to 60% range may describe some seasons, but it doesn't adequately reflect the variability we see over time," said study senior author Dr. Justin Ortiz, a researcher at the university's Center for Vaccine Development and Global Health.

The trick, he said, is "to communicate that uncertainty without losing sight of the substantial benefits of vaccination."

The findings were recently published in JAMA Network Open.

In the study, Ortiz's team looked at end-of-season estimates of flu vaccine effectiveness for flu seasons from 2004 to 2005 through 2023 to 2024. They also looked at whether a particular season's vaccine was well matched to the flu strains that actually appeared.

The team found that influenza vaccines had a median effectiveness of 39.5% in preventing flu infection. That's below the 40% to 60% effectiveness range typically cited by public health officials and media, researchers noted. (Median means some years' protection was greater and some years' less.)

They noted that higher estimates of effectiveness are often predicated on the notion that the flu vaccine is a good match for circulating strains of the virus. However, the study showed it often wasn't the case: In 11 of the 18 tracked seasons, vaccines did not match circulating strains.

None of this means flu shots are useless, and Ortiz's team stressed that shots are still the most effective means Americans have of preventing influenza, which kills between 6,300 and 52,000 people each year, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

And this year, flu is spreading early, accounting for 2,100 deaths so far this season. The CDC estimates that, during the 2023 to 2024 flu season, vaccination saved 7,900 lives. It also prevented 120,000 flu-related hospitalizations and 9.8 million flu-related illnesses.

It's hoped the new data will help spur research into improving influenza vaccines so they offer broader protection against the ever-mutating virus.

"The message is clear that annual flu shots remain our best option for now as we continue to develop vaccines that provide more predictable and lasting protection," said study lead author Dr. Matthew Wolpert, an internal medicine resident at the University of Maryland Medical Center.

Publication details

Matthew D. Wolpert et al., Testing the 40% to 60% Influenza Vaccine Effectiveness Heuristic, JAMA Network Open (2026). DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.42906

Journal information: JAMA Network Open

item.title: Your genes might boost risk for high cholesterol
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Your genes might boost risk for high cholesterol

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

Frustrated that your cholesterol levels aren't budging for the better? You may have your genes to blame, a new study finds.

Researchers at Stanford University found certain genes influenced, for good or ill, how women's bodies dealt with cholesterol.

It's an issue plaguing millions of health-conscious Americans.

"We have people who come into clinic and say, 'I changed my diet and it made no difference in my cholesterol.' Or they say, 'I changed my diet and it had a huge effect on my cholesterol,'" noted senior author Dr. Shoa Clarke, a cardiologist and assistant professor of medicine and pediatrics at Stanford Medicine.

His team's findings are not meant to deter folks from fighting cholesterol, however.

"Sometimes people think, 'Oh, if I'm genetically prone to something, then it doesn't really matter what my diet is or what the environment is like; it's genetically predetermined.' But what we're saying here is the opposite," Clarke said in a news release. "The people who had this genetic predisposition for higher LDL ['bad' cholesterol] were actually the ones with the most sensitivity to diet, where diet has the best chance of helping them—or hurting them, if the diet is not good."

The findings were published Nov. 18 in the journal JACC: Advances.

The new study looked at data collected for decades among more than 21,000 American women, as part of the ongoing Women's Health Initiative.

At the study's beginning in 1991, the women's median age was 65, meaning half were younger and half were older. About half were White, a third were Black and 15% were Hispanic.

All checked in regularly with detailed reports on their daily diet, and all of the women got regular cholesterol checks.

Most importantly for this study, the women also underwent complex genetic analysis.

The Stanford team found that certain genes seem to predispose women to higher levels of cholesterol, and that was especially true for women who consumed high levels of unhealthy saturated fats. For women lacking these genes, no such association was found.

Further research showed that women who ranked in the top 25% in terms of a genetic propensity for high LDL cholesterol and saturated fat intake were also much more prone to suffer a stroke or heart attack.

The other 75% (with a less pronounced genetic predisposition) did not seem as affected by saturated fat intake, the team noted.

"We found the same thing—that the association between saturated fat intake and risk for having cardiovascular events was amplified for those people at the upper end of the genetic spectrum," Clarke said. "This variation in response to saturated fat may be one of the reasons there is so much controversy and disagreement over how much is OK in a diet."

The study is in line with guidelines from the World Health Organization urging people to limit their intake of red meat, because it contains high levels of saturated fat.

Clarke's team found that—despite what fans of high-fat ketogenic diets might claim—higher saturated fat intake offered no protective effect for the heart, even among those at relatively low genetic risk for higher LDL cholesterol.

"The effects of saturated fat may not be the same for everyone, but there isn't any evidence of a cardiovascular benefit to eating more saturated fat," Clarke said. "The harms might vary from small to large depending on who you are."

In prior research, the Stanford group created a "polygenic risk score" assessing an individual's relative odds for poor heart health based on their genetics.

"We don't yet have evidence that polygenic risk scores should be used to guide diet recommendations," Clarke said. "But that certainly is a future area of study, and from what our results in this new study suggest, could indeed be a fruitful one."

More information

Alexa Barad et al., Association Between Saturated Fat Intake and Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol Across the Genetic Spectrum, JACC: Advances (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.jacadv.2026.103423

item.title: Democrats Demand Answers From Oz After Delay in $50B Rural Health Awards
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Democrats Demand Answers From Oz After Delay in $50B Rural Health Awards

Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a nine-day delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans.

Saying rural care is “in an acute state of crisis,” 18 members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz late Thursday. The letter pointed to what it called “an alarming lack of public transparency” and said the fund “lacks sufficient guardrails to protect rural hospitals at greatest risk of closure.”

Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski said her state “got no explanation from CMS as to why” it got $3 million less in its second-year Rural Health Transformation Program allocation. It was a roughly 1.5% reduction from its $193.4 million first-year award. State leaders have not received information about an appeals process, she said.

Any delay in knowing how much they received and any reduction in their base funding is significant, Budzinski said, because states need to plan for an “acute impact” from the loss of other federal funding.

In the first year, states competed for their initial share of the $50 billion, which is handed out at $10 billion a year for five years. They won awards ranging from $147 million to $281 million. Most of the lawmakers who signed the letter were from states that lost funding this year. Rep. Terri Sewell of Alabama, which got $4.1 million less, along with Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado, which saw a nearly $3 million drop, also spearheaded the letter along with Budzinski.

One concern, Budzinski said, is “making sure that the money isn’t going to consultants, that it’s actually getting to the rural providers that it is supposed to be getting to.” The lawmakers asked Oz for a response to detailed questions by Nov. 25. They also requested a briefing about the delays to the funding announcement, which was first reported by KFF Health News, and the impact on states.

The second-year awards were due to be announced by Oct. 31, but an Oct. 30 letter from CMS stated officials “discovered an additional administrative process requirement.” Instead, second-year funding was announced Nov. 9.

“Those kind of delays prevent a state to fully prepare for what’s to come,” Budzinski said.

CMS oversees the fund and its newly formed Office of Rural Health Transformation. Agency officials did not respond to questions for this article before the given deadline.

Republicans passed the Rural Health Transformation Program last summer as a last-minute sweetener to offset other ramifications of President Donald Trump’s signature budget law, including an estimated $137 billion in Medicaid spending cuts for rural America over 10 years.

That rural money is “retail therapy for Congress,” said Cara James, president and chief executive of Grantmakers in Health, while speaking at a Milken Institute event this month.

Because the same tax law cut Medicaid spending, which rural hospitals and people disproportionately use, as well as supplemental food assistance and other government grants, the short-term money would not “help sustain people” in rural America, James said.

Then, she posed a persistent fear about the fund: “If it’s even getting to the communities.”

Five rural hospitals have closed or been converted into lower-level facilities since the rural fund was created, including one in Michigan that shuttered beds and switched to providing only emergency services to survive, according to a list curated by the Cecil G. Sheps Center for Health Services Research at the University of North Carolina.

The letter stated lawmakers’ concerns that too much of the rural fund “could flow to large consulting and technology firms rather than supporting providers and communities on the ground.”

After the law passed last year, state leaders had just over seven weeks to write applications as they competed for the first-year funds. All 50 states won funding with allocations determined by a federal scoring process. Each year, officials are to revisit the funding allotments.

Most states saw their funding change by less than 2%. North Dakota and Iowa won the largest gains; New Jersey, Florida, and Vermont saw the biggest reductions.

Although federal officials have created state data maps, released a slew of press announcements, and led sessions on the complicated scoring of state applications, it’s not enough, said Alan Morgan, CEO of the National Rural Health Association.

The association, which represents hospitals and community clinics nationwide, sent its own letter to federal officials Nov. 9. Morgan said that the way states win money needs “to be articulated in a way that success can be replicated by all states going forward.”

Morgan said his association’s analysis found that state leaders are sending the federal money to local hospitals and clinics because communities and individuals are “relying on rural hospitals to be there to deliver care.” But it’s unclear, he said, how much of the overall rural fund local hospitals are actually receiving versus how much is benefiting other entities, such as consultants.

In their letter, Budzinski and the other Democrats asked if CMS would establish a searchable database that tracks spending. They also asked for an explanation of how federal officials will evaluate state performance and allocate awards.

It was just the latest congressional letter to federal health officials on this issue.

In August 2025, a month after the law passed, Democrats sent a letter about the program’s rollout to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. And last November, Budzinski reached out to Oz on behalf of Illinois. Bennet, along with Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and others, signed a letter in June asking that the funds be targeted to rescue rural hospitals and clinics.

“We haven’t gotten full responses to any of these inquiries,” said Budzinski, who will become chair of the House’s largest Democratic caucus, the New Democrat Coalition, as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.

item.title: Hair pulling, skin picking and nail biting are common in young people and cause significant distress
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Hair pulling, skin picking and nail biting are common in young people and cause significant distress

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

The study found that body-focused repetitive behaviors (BFRBs), as they are known, can be a significant source of distress, particularly among young people who also experienced anxiety, depression and bullying.

Researchers asked more than 5,400 school students ages 11 to 18, mainly in Oxfordshire and Liverpool, questions about BFRBs as part of the larger OxWell Student Survey. Those who had experienced BFRBs were asked to what extent those behaviors upset or distressed them, ranging from 'not at all' to 'a great deal."

The data, published in BMJ Mental Health, showed:

- In the sample, 58.5% of young people reported at least one BFRB.

- These behaviors were a significant source of distress for 13% (answering that they caused 'quite a lot' or 'a great deal' of distress or upset).

- The most commonly reported behavior was nail biting (43.6%), followed by skin picking (31.3%) and hair pulling (14.5%), with 17.6% of those experiencing BFRBs reporting two or more.

- Hair pulling and skin picking were associated with substantially higher levels of distress than nail biting (37% and 29%, respectively, versus 11%).

- Girls and transgender/gender-diverse young people were substantially more likely than boys both to experience BFRBs and to find them distressing. Around one in four transgender/gender-diverse young people and one in six girls reported distressing BFRBs, compared with around one in 18 boys.

- More than a third of young people with anxiety and depression (34%) had experienced distressing BFRBs, as well as 27% of those who had experienced bullying.

The researchers also found that distressing BFRBs were reported by around one in five young people who identified as autistic or having ADHD—approximately twice the rate seen in those without these conditions. This difference was largely explained by higher levels of emotional distress and experiences of bullying, rather than neurodivergence itself.

Lead author professor Clare Mackay from the University of Oxford's Department of Psychiatry, who has experienced BFRBs herself, said, "These findings show that BFRBs are common in adolescents, and that they are strongly associated with emotional distress and social adversity. This distress often goes unrecognized because these types of behaviors are rarely discussed in schools, health care or wider society, and so those experiencing them often have little support.

"BFRBs aren't simply bad habits. They're often signs that a young person is struggling. Asking whether someone ever pulls, picks or bites at themselves in a way that upsets them could open an important conversation. If we recognize these behaviors earlier, we have a much better chance of offering support before they become entrenched."

Co-author professor Polly Waite, deputy director of the Oxford Centre for Emerging Minds Research and co-lead for the NIHR Biomedical Research Centre: Oxford Health's Mental Health in Development Theme, said, "This research highlights the need for better support for young people with BFRBs. Shame and stigma can make it difficult for young people to talk about these behaviors or seek help. We need to open up conversations about BFRBs, challenge the stigma surrounding them, and help young people realize they are not alone."

The data came from the OxWell Student Survey, which is conducted every two years. The findings are shared back with schools to inform policy and practice, as well as with local authorities to guide education and mental health provision, and to shape national policy on education and well-being.

The findings follow another recent qualitative study highlighting the central role of shame in young people who experience hair pulling. Twelve adolescents took part in semistructured interviews, which found that shame was an enduring emotion that triggered, maintained and exacerbated hair pulling. The findings were published in the journal Psychology and Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice.

Publication details

Clare Mackay et al., Body-focused repetitive behaviours are common, distressing and under-recognised: a cross-sectional study from the OxWell Student Survey, BMJ Mental Health (2026). DOI: 10.1136/bmjment-2026-302871

Laura A. F. Lee et al., Tangled in shame: A qualitative exploration of shame in adolescent hairpulling, Psychology and Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice (2026). DOI: 10.1111/papt.70114

Journal information: BMJ Mental Health

Source: Medical Xpress | Published: 2026-11-20 21:20 UTC

item.title: ICE detention of Princeton scientist rattles academia
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

A graduate student who is a scientific researcher at Princeton University was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement earlier this week while traveling home after presenting research at the annual Society for Neuroscience conference in Washington, D.C.

The researcher, Eva Yi Xie, was detained Thursday. Although she has lived in the U.S. since 2016 after moving to the country from China, her visa had expired, according to The New York Times. Her lawyers told a reporter Xie had a pending asylum application and was thus allowed to remain in the country legally.

The news, first posted by a mentor of Xie’s on X, ricocheted across academic circles on Friday, in part because it seemed to crystalize pervasive fears of non-U.S. academics and international students that traveling to conferences to present new research and network with colleagues may be too risky during a second Trump administration that has cracked down on immigration.

“There’s, I think, an open question about whether or not it’s safe for people who are international students on visas to travel, because there have been these detentions, and that’s a very scary prospect,” said Caitlin Rivers, a John Hopkins academic who said a staff member of hers was detained by ICE earlier this year. A number of U.S. conferences have reported smaller attendance over the past two years, and some have considered hosting in other countries.

ICE did not respond to a request for comment as to why Xie was detained. But the administration has been vocal in its desire to reduce the number of foreign-born graduate students in the U.S. In its science blueprint released earlier this year, the White House wrote “America’s over-reliance on foreign students also creates a security challenge.”

Xie is not the first graduate student to be detained. In one notable instance, Tufts researcher Rumeysa Ozturk was detained by ICE last year in Cambridge, Mass., and later decided to leave the country. A report released earlier this week found that international graduate student enrollment is down by a third at academic medical centers.

“News of Eva’s detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community,” Rodney D. Priestley, the dean of Princeton University’s graduate school, wrote in a statement, adding the university has provided Xie with legal representation. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”

Xie’s work lies at the intersection of neuroscience and artificial intelligence; she uses a combination of experiments on mice and large datasets of neural recordings to understand how different portions of the brain work together to make decisions. A third-year PhD student, she is viewed as a rising star by some of her colleagues.

“I think it speaks to how exceptional of a researcher Eva is that she can work on projects that really span multiple disciplines, that require that she go and learn the foundations, not just of AI and machine learning, and not just computational models of the brain, but also understanding how do you run the experiment on the mice. She’s in the lab actually doing the surgery on the mice, gathering the data from the mice, analyzing those data, and running the AI experiments,” said Benjamin Eysenbach, a computer scientist at Princeton and one of Xie’s advisers.

As an example of the respect she commands among peers, Eysenbach cited a workshop she convened at last year’s NeurIPS conference, one of the premiere machine learning conferences. Xie presented research of her own, and also brought together leaders in AI and in neuroscience to see how they could collaborate.

It was an opportunity both to “introduce these important questions about the brain to folks in AI that might be equipped with new methods, and to help folks working on neuroscience questions define what are the right AI tools,” Eysenbach said.

Krithik Ramesh, a fellow researcher, is among those who has benefitted from her guidance. The two had overlapped at science fair competitions throughout high school, and when Ramesh was considering transferring to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where Xie had completed her undergraduate degree, he turned to her for counsel. He learned about Xie’s detention after a friend saw a post on social media. His immediate reaction was disbelief, followed by a sense of unmooring as a fellow researcher.

“We academics exist for the benefit of the public,” he said. “We are very privileged as a country to have people like Eva continue to pursue academia at the highest level, and to share that with other people. That’s literally the nature and reason why we go to conferences to present stuff. It is appalling to me that she cannot do that with reasonable certainty that she can’t be detained.”

Source: STAT | Published: 2026-11-20 21:19 UTC
